hints: Sort the five solids first by what particles are in the lattice: metal ions, oppositely charged ions, atoms joined in a network, or separate small molecules.
Recall which two of the list exist as discrete $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{I}_2$ molecules held together only by intermolecular forces.
Recall which solid is the classic network covalent oxide with only $\text{Si-O}$ bonds extending in three dimensions, like diamond.
Decide for copper whether the bonding involves delocalised electrons around positive ions, and for sodium chloride whether it involves a regular array of cations and anions.
Match each bonding type to its lattice word: giant for continuous networks of ions, atoms or metal ions, simple or molecular for separate molecules.
walkthrough:
Picture what sits on the lattice points**
Think particle by particle. Copper has $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Sodium chloride has $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions. Silicon(IV) oxide has $\text{Si}$ and $\text{O}$ atoms joined by strong covalent bonds throughout. Ice has whole $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules and iodine has whole $\text{I}_2$ molecules. That picture already tells you the bonding.

Assign the bonding type**
Copper must be metallic. Sodium chloride must be ionic. Silicon(IV) oxide, ice and iodine all contain covalent bonds inside the molecules or network. For ice you can also describe the important attraction between molecules as hydrogen bonding.

Decide giant or simple**
Ask: does the bonding continue endlessly or stop at a small molecule? Copper, $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{NaCl}$ go on in three dimensions, so they are giant. Ice and iodine stop at $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{I}_2$, with only weak intermolecular forces between the molecules, so they are simple molecular.

Final answer: copper: metallic bonding; giant / metallic lattice
ice: covalent (hydrogen bonding accepted for bonding); simple / molecular / hydrogen-bonded lattice
silicon(IV) oxide: covalent bonding; giant / macromolecular lattice
iodine: covalent bonding; simple / molecular lattice
sodium chloride: ionic bonding; giant / ionic lattice

hints: Think why ice has a much higher melting point than expected for such a small molecule, and which special force needs H attached to N, O or F.
walkthrough:
Link water structure to its strongest force**
In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, H is directly bonded to very electronegative O, and O has lone pairs. That is exactly the condition for the strongest intermolecular force, hydrogen bonding, which holds the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules together in ice.

hints: Start by drawing two bent $\text{H-O-H}$ molecules side by side, with O showing two lone pairs and H showing no lone pairs.
Remember a hydrogen bond always joins the lone pair on one molecule to the H already covalently bonded in the other molecule.
Consider what labels an examiner needs to see to know you understand polarity: partial charges on O and H, covalent bond vs H-bond line style, and the lone pair involved.
walkthrough:
Draw two correct water molecules**
Draw two bent $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules. Each O has two $\text{O-H}$ covalent bonds drawn as solid lines and two lone pairs drawn as pairs of dots. The bent shape matters because it leaves the lone pairs exposed.

Make the H-bond in the right place**
Join them as $\text{O-H}----\text{O}$. The H-bond goes from the H of one molecule to the O of the different molecule. Use a dashed or dotted line for the H-bond so it is clearly different from the solid covalent $\text{O-H}$ bond.

Add polarity and the lone pair**
Label $^{\delta-}$ on O and $^{\delta+}$ on H to show the permanent dipole that causes the attraction. Show at least three partial charges in a row, for example $^{\delta-}\text{O}-\text{H}^{\delta+}----^{\delta-}\text{O}$. Finally draw the lone pair on the accepting O directly in line with the $\text{H}----\text{O}$ bond, because the H-bond is the attraction of that lone pair for the $^{\delta+}$ H.

Final answer: Diagram shows $^{\delta-}\text{O}-\text{H}^{\delta+}----^{\delta-}\text{O}$ between two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules.
Covalent $\text{O-H}$ shown as solid line, $\text{H}----\text{O}$ hydrogen bond as dashed line.
Partial charges $^{\delta-}$ on both O atoms and $^{\delta+}$ on H atoms involved, with a lone pair on the accepting O in line with the H-bond.

hints: Use the melting point of copper, $1085^{\circ}\text{C}$, to work out what $T_1$ on the flat part must be.
Recall what is present before freezing starts, during the flat freezing plateau, and after freezing is complete.
walkthrough:
Read the shape of the cooling curve**
From $1200^{\circ}\text{C}$ down to $T_1$ the temperature falls, so in X no change of state is happening. $T_1$ must be the freezing point, $1085^{\circ}\text{C}$. The flat part Y is freezing, and the falling part Z is cooling of the formed solid.

Assign the states**
In X the copper is still above its melting point, so liquid only. In Y liquid is turning to solid, so both liquid and solid are present together. In Z freezing is finished, so solid only.

Final answer: X = liquid (molten copper only)
Y = liquid and solid (both present during freezing)
Z = solid (copper only)

hints: Link falling temperature in stage X directly to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Picture how ions in liquid copper move when cooled but not yet frozen: speed and freedom to slide past each other.
walkthrough:
Connect temperature to energy**
Temperature measures average kinetic energy. In stage X the graph slopes down, heat is lost to the surroundings, so the average kinetic energy of the copper particles falls.

Describe the motion**
With less kinetic energy the particles move more slowly. They still slide past each other because it is still liquid, but their speed and amount of movement decrease as cooling continues.

Final answer: Kinetic energy of particles is decreasing.
Movement / motion of particles is slowing down.

hints: Think what bonds or attractions are forming as mobile liquid particles lock into a regular solid lattice.
Consider the energy change for bond formation, exothermic or endothermic, and how released heat affects the temperature reading while heat is still being lost.
walkthrough:
Spot that freezing builds bonds**
In stage Y liquid copper becomes solid copper. Particles that were moving freely lock into a fixed metallic lattice. Forming these metallic bonds releases energy, so freezing is exothermic.

Balance heat loss with heat release**
The sample is still losing heat to the surroundings, which would normally lower the temperature. But the heat released by bond formation replaces that lost heat almost exactly. With no net change in kinetic energy, the temperature stays flat at $T_1$ until all the liquid has frozen.

Final answer: Bond formation during freezing releases energy / is exothermic.
This released energy compensates for the heat loss by cooling, so temperature remains constant at $T_1$.
